title: What machine learning is

sections.title: 1.2 A model is a small picture of the world
1.5 AI, machine learning, deep learning, LLMs
1.7 When not to use machine learning

html:
Purpose. Before any formula, you need to know what problem machine learning solves and when it is the right tool. Every later technique hangs on this idea.

Key ideas

  • Ordinary software follows rules a person wrote. Machine learning finds the rules itself from examples.
  • A model is a function that turns inputs into a prediction. Learning means choosing the numbers inside it (its parameters) so that its predictions match the examples.
  • There are two phases: training (fit the parameters) and inference (use the fitted model on new inputs).
  • Good data matters more than a clever algorithm.

1.1 Rules versus examples

Imagine you must teach a new colleague to spot loan applications that will not be repaid. You have two options. The first is a rulebook: "decline if income is below X, or if the debt ratio is above Y". The second is to hand over 10,000 past files with their outcomes and let them develop a feel for it. Machine learning is the second option, done by a computer.

Arthur Samuel gave the classic definition in 1959: machine learning is the field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed. His checkers program played tens of thousands of games against itself and ended up playing better than he did (Ng, video 3). Nobody wrote its strategy. It found one.

This matters because some problems have too many rules to write. Nobody can list the rules that separate spam from real mail, recognise a voice, or rank web pages. For those problems, examples work and rulebooks do not.

1.2 A model is a small picture of the world

When you see dark clouds and predict rain, you are using a mental model. A model in machine learning is the same thing written as a function: inputs go in, a prediction comes out. The simplest useful one is a straight line:

tomorrow’s temperature=m×today’s temperature+b\text{tomorrow's temperature} = m \times \text{today's temperature} + b

The numbers m and b are the parameters. They decide whether the predictions are any good. "Learning" is the search for the m and b that fit the examples best (Shaw Talebi, ML Foundations).

1.3 Training and inference

Phase What happens Cost Analogy
Training The parameters are fitted to example data Slow, done once or now and then Going to school
Inference The fitted model predicts for a new input Fast, done all the time Doing the job

When people say a model "costs" a lot, they usually mean training. When your app answers a customer, that is inference.

1.4 Three ways to learn

  • Supervised learning: every example comes with the right answer. The model learns to map inputs to answers. Most business ML is this.
  • Unsupervised learning: there are no answers. The model looks for structure by itself, such as groups of similar customers.
  • Reinforcement learning: the model tries actions and gets a reward or a penalty. It learns by trial and error. AlphaGo used it, and so did the training of reasoning models such as DeepSeek R1, which were rewarded for correct maths and code answers.

Chapter 2 covers all three in detail. Deep learning is not a fourth way to learn. It is a kind of model, a neural network with many layers, that can be trained in any of the three ways, most often the first.

1.5 AI, machine learning, deep learning, LLMs

These terms nest like Russian dolls. Artificial intelligence is the broad goal. Machine learning is the part of it that learns from data. Deep learning is the part of machine learning that uses large neural networks. A large language model (LLM) is a deep network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word, then refined with supervised examples and reinforcement learning. This book moves in that order: classical machine learning first, because LLMs reuse its ideas.

1.6 Where machine learning is used

You already use it many times a day: web search ranking, tagging friends in photos, movie recommendations, voice assistants and spam filters. In industry it optimizes wind turbines, helps doctors diagnose, and inspects products on factory lines with computer vision (Ng, videos 1 and 2). Ng quotes McKinsey's estimate that AI and machine learning could add about $13 trillion of value per year by 2030, much of it outside software: retail, travel, transport and manufacturing. He also says artificial general intelligence, machines as smart as people, is overhyped and still far away.

1.7 When not to use machine learning

Beyond the videos. Machine learning is not always the answer:

  • If the rule is clear and stable, write the rule. "The borrower must be 18 or older" is a rule, not a prediction.
  • If you have no data, or only a handful of examples, a model has nothing to learn from.
  • If a wrong prediction is very costly and nobody can explain it, you need extra safeguards, or a simpler model.
  • Always try a trivial baseline first (Chapter 3). If a clever model barely beats it, the clever model is not worth its cost.

1.8 The workflow in one list

  1. Define the problem as a prediction: what is the input, and what is the answer?
  2. Collect and clean the data.
  3. Choose the inputs (features) and how to prepare them (Chapter 8).
  4. Train a model (Chapters 4 to 7, 9 and 10).
  5. Evaluate it on data it has never seen (Chapters 3 and 12).
  6. Deploy it, watch it, and retrain when the world changes.

Loan example. Rules handle the legal checks: is the applicant of age, is the amount within the product limit. A model handles the questions with no clean rule: "how likely is this applicant to accept our offer?" and "what will this offer cost per month?" The first needs a classifier (Chapter 9), the second a regression (Chapter 7).

Common mistakes

  • Using machine learning where a rule would do, and then having to maintain a model nobody can explain.
  • Judging a model by how well it does on the data it was trained on (Chapter 3).
  • Spending weeks on the algorithm when the data is wrong.

Check yourself

  • Explain the difference between a rule-based system and a machine learning system, using a loan example.
  • Name the two phases of a model's life and say which one is expensive.
  • Is deep learning a way to learn, like supervised learning? Explain.
  • Give one task in a bank where you would write a rule instead of training a model.
Show answers

(1) A rule-based system applies rules a person wrote; a learning system finds the pattern from past files and their outcomes. (2) Training and inference; training is the expensive one. (3) No. It is a type of model that can be trained in any of the three ways. (4) For example checking that an applicant is of legal age.
